claimed.text: Lacatski, Kelleher and Knapp describe AAWSAP's Utah field operations, physiological effects on personnel, and Lacatski's own account of entering a craft of unknown origin; the book describes federally funded collection of poltergeist-type activity, apparitions and animal effects at the ranch.

By the co-authors' account, the programme began when Lacatski read Kelleher and Knapp's Hunt for the Skinwalker, visited the ranch, reported an experience there and Bigelow relayed it to Senator Reid. Knapp is credited with introducing Reid to Bigelow in the first place, so the reporter, the contractor's deputy and the programme manager are also the authors of the account.

The leaked BAASS Ten Month Report describes the property under 24-hour surveillance with rapid-response patrols. Knapp has said BAASS recruited about 50 cleared investigators, ran for 27 months and built a 240,000-case database designed by Vallee, most of whose papers DIA has never released.
Bigelow said in 1998 that anomalous aerial activity and unusual animal deaths had continued on and around the property, and that they would not be there just for the weather.

Science reported that Travis Taylor was chief scientist of the UAP Task Force. Current ranch owner Brandon Fugal says Taylor was called to that post largely because of his work at the ranch, where he had arrived a sceptic, and that the ranch team did not know of the appointment until he was cleared to disclose it.

Fugal also says Sean Kirkpatrick sat through a confidential briefing on the ranch in April 2018 despite later saying he had never attended one, and that he published a photograph of Kirkpatrick there.
Author Peter Levenda says that when he asked Puthoff, Vallee and Mellon about the ranch's equipment and data, all three fell silent and Puthoff said the question needed a secure facility.

contested.text: NIDS investigators, including John Alexander, examined close to 100 incidents at the ranch but acknowledged they could not obtain evidence fit for scientific publication.
Barry Greenwood published a critical review of Skinwalkers at the Pentagon in the Journal of Scientific Exploration in 2023.

DIA cannot find the ranch report or the 2007 letter in a programme whose contract required monthly status reports, which the board reads as the field record having been kept by the contractor or never filed.

The board infers an unreconciled inconsistency: DoD cleared a manuscript in which its former programme manager describes entering a craft of unknown origin, while maintaining there is no evidence of such craft.

On the board's reading, federal money paid for continuous monitoring of a property owned by the prime contractor's principal, a contracting-integrity question no oversight body has examined; and the government did not build a capability but bought one, with a site chosen from a regional folk record rather than military sensor data.
The records disagree on the size of the ranch, one giving a 480-acre parcel and another about 512 acres.

No government organisation chart naming Taylor as the task force's chief scientist has been released, and the board notes that he applied near-identical sensing methods inside the task force and on a television production at the ranch with no public account of what passed between the two.

lead.text: Skinwalker Ranch in Utah's Uintah Basin was bought in 1996 by Robert Bigelow, whose privately funded National Institute for Discovery Science ran an instrumented field station there, and it was later investigated under DIA's AAWSAP contract. The Pentagon's own 2024 history confirms that investigation of what it calls an alleged hotspot of UAP and paranormal activity, but DIA cannot locate the report it produced.

record.text: AARO's 2024 history states that AAWSAP/AATIP investigated an alleged hotspot of UAP and paranormal activity at a Utah property then owned by the head of the contractor, and that the contractor team conducted UAP and paranormal research there under a special appropriation.

Bigelow bought the property in 1996 from Terry and Gwen Sherman, who as a condition of sale agreed to keep quiet about what they had witnessed; the sale was reported at the time and Bigelow confirmed the condition in 1998. He owned the ranch throughout the DIA contract.

DIA could locate no records of the report titled Utah Ranch Investigation: August 2009-February 2010, nor of the June 2007 Lacatski letter to Bigelow described in the book; an appeal also returned nothing.
The manuscript of Skinwalkers at the Pentagon was cleared for publication through DoD prepublication review.
DIA's August 2008 AAWSAP solicitation, contract file, statement of work and deliverables have been released under FOIA.
The New Yorker records that among the consultants Bigelow hired at NIDS was Hal Puthoff, whose paranormal work dated back to Project Stargate.
AARO's history also names Bigelow's organisation as the anticipated contract performer for the proposed KONA BLUE programme, whose material it says was only assumed to exist.

summary.text: Bigelow founded NIDS in 1995 as a privately funded institute researching aerial phenomena, animal mutilations and related anomalies. It is reported to have run a public reporting line and to have sent veterinarians to perform necropsies on reported mutilations at no cost to ranchers, and Bigelow is reported to have shut it down in 2004 while keeping the ranch.

NIDS is reported to have drawn on figures from government science: Colm Kelleher ran its field operations as deputy administrator, John Alexander and Jacques Vallee sat on its boards, Kit Green served on its science advisory board and Eric Davis worked there as a scientist; The New Yorker records that Hal Puthoff was hired as a consultant.

The ranch is the link from the private institute to the Pentagon: by the account of Lacatski and his co-authors a DIA official wrote to Bigelow about it in 2007, though DIA has found no record of the letter; the AAWSAP contract went to BAASS in 2008, reportedly with substantially the same people, and AARO confirms that AAWSAP funded investigation of the site.
The insider account of that work, Skinwalkers at the Pentagon by Lacatski, Kelleher and Knapp, was published in 2021 after DoD prepublication review.
